title: Pointers: Address, Indirection and the Double Pointer
quickIdea: A pointer is a typed box that holds an address. & produces an address, * follows one, and each extra star follows one more level.
remember: int x = 12; int *p = &x; int **q = &p; then p holds &x, *p is 12, *q is p, and **q is 12. Count the stars to count the levels.
A pointer has a type: p + 1 on an int * moves sizeof(int) bytes, and a pointer of one type must be cast before it is dereferenced as another.
A pointer parameter is a copied address. It can change the pointee but not the caller's pointer variable; passing int ** is how a function reassigns the caller's pointer.

An uninitialised pointer is a wild pointer and dereferencing it is undefined behaviour; a pointer to a released or returned object is dangling and equally undefined. NULL is the only value you may test before dereferencing.
char *s = "GATE"; may point at a read-only literal, so s[0] = 'L' is undefined behaviour; char s[] = "GATE"; makes a writable copy.

example.prompt: int f(int x, int *py, int **ppz) { int y, z; **ppz += 1; z = **ppz; *py += 2; y = *py; x += 3; return x + y + z; } with c = 4, b = &c, a = &b and the call f(c, b, a).
example.work: Both *py and **ppz reach c, and x is only a copy. **ppz += 1 makes c = 5, and z = 5. *py += 2 makes c = 7, and y = 7. x is still the copy 4, so x += 3 makes x = 7. The return value is 7 + 7 + 5 = 19.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2008 Q.60 is this function, printed as 19. The whole question is the difference between the copy x and the two pointers that alias c. GATE CSE 2024 Set 2 Q.23 asks the neighbouring question of what a function returning b - a means when b has walked to the NUL.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: int x = 12; int *p = &x; int **q = &p; **q = 20; what is x?
variations.answer: 20 - **q names the object that q reaches through p, so the write lands on x.
variations.why: The same alias chain as the 2008 question with the arithmetic removed, so only the level counting is tested.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does a function that allocates and hands back memory take a char ** parameter?
variations.answer: Because it has to change the caller's pointer variable. The parameter is a copy of an address, so only by passing the address of the pointer itself can the function write a new address into the caller's variable.
variations.why: Explains the double pointer from the side of design rather than of tracing, which is how questions about malloc wrappers are phrased.

trap.what: Expecting a variable to track another because a pointer to it exists.
trap.why: Aliasing is one-way. A write through the pointer changes the object, but a copy taken before the write keeps the old value, and a plain parameter is exactly such a copy.
trap.counterexample: In GATE CSE 2008 Q.60, x was initialised from c = 4 and stays a separate object, so x += 3 gives 7 from the copy 4, not 10 from the c that has already become 7.

check.question: int a = 5; int *p = &a; int **q = &p; what do *q and **q evaluate to?
check.answer: *q is the address of a, that is the value of p, and **q is 5.
check.explanation: Each * follows one stored address: q holds &p, so the first star reaches p and the second reaches a.
